newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines catches up tigers a little late.
newsitem.headline: Philippines catches up tigers a little late.

text.p: After decades of mismanagement, the Philippines had finally started to catch up with the rest of Asia's economic tigers, and even its Finance Secretary, Roberto de Ocampo, had begun calling himself "Tiger Bobby."
But rather like a guest arriving at a party when the others are going home, the Philippines has joined the pack just as the glitter of Southeast Asia was starting to fade.
On Friday, it became the latest Asian country to surrender to relentless attacks on its currency, forced to stand by as the market dragged the peso down 11.5 percent against the dollar.

Now economists and analysts warn that the Philippines and its mostly poor population of 70 million, only just beginning to enjoy the first fruits of economic success, face a very fragile few months with the certainty of higher inflation and slower growth.
"There is a real danger of panic in the market and widespread public discontent as purchasing power plunges," the daily Philippine Star said in an editorial on Sunday.
"The government must make sure it has a better grip on these potentially explosive scenarios than it has on the peso. We have been handed a bitter pill. Can it save us?" it said.
President Fidel Ramos appealed to Filipinos to react calmly and said things would settle down in a few days.

Government officials hope the de facto devaluation, the second in the region in as many weeks after Thailand's, will be enough to send speculators on the scent of blood elsewhere while it licks its wounds.
Malaysia appears set to be the next victim of the repeated speculative currency attacks that are prompting fund managers to look to other emerging regions such as Latin America to park their money.
Manila's central bank spent an estimated $2 billion -- money the country needs to pay for imports -- and sent interest rates up to punitive levels in its failed defence of the peso.
Many economists felt it should have done it much earlier.

"(The peso fall) should not have been this sudden if it was done by our authorities five years ago. It was like a tooth decay, if you don't seek medication now maybe you will need an extraction later," said former Economic Planning Secretary Solita Monsod.
The immediate impact will be to spark inflation in a country that relies almost entirely on imports for its fuel.
Since Ramos came to power in 1992, the country has at last shaken off its image as the "sick man of Asia", and begun to show high growth and promise of sustained prosperity.
It was only after Ramos' success with the economy that decades of often brutal communist insurgency began to dwindle.

"What might disturb the economy in the long term is inflation because this would kick up to near double digits...but this will gradually adjust," said University of the Philippines political science professor Alex Magno.
On the plus side is the prospect of even faster growth in now more competitive exports that will boost industry.
There will, however, be political costs, which come in the last year of Ramos' presidency when a crowd of candidates are already campaigning to replace him.
Many consider the person Ramos eventually picks to succeed him as the most likely winner in next May's election.
"It is politically costly...there will be a price shock, but it's better for Ramos to do these price shocks now," Magno said.

He hoped portfolio investors would now return to the Philippines, which would have the benefit of giving the economy investment- rather than consumer-backed drive. He said the inevitable hike in inflation would not cause permanent damage.

"We expect the carpet-baggers to come in and correct the situation, the same people who put pressure on the peso by withdrawing from the stock market. It's a speculative game. Unfortunately, nobody can control it."
"The pressure is off us now. You had this eyes-on-the- Philippines situation before. Now everybody will be waiting for (Malaysia)...to do the same; the domino effect," Magno said.
Political analyst Amando Doronila said the long-term impact should in fact be helpful and that with the expected higher exports, Ramos should be able to create more jobs.
"But it's a razor-edge situation. This is delicate and the events in the next few weeks will determine the bad effects of devaluation and whether adjustments can be made," Doronila said.
